findings.paper_title: ESCW Q1 Revenue Budget Monitoring 202627 Report
findings.headline: £575k of non-recurring resources supporting Additional Support for Learning staffing expansion
findings.detail: Additional Support for Learning is receiving £575k of non-recurring funding to provide 1,208 additional hours of staffing support beyond the recurring budget allocation of 10,927 hours. The paper describes this as an 'agreed use' but does not address how this will be funded in future years if demand remains at this level.
findings.matters: When recurring services rely on non-recurring funding for operational expansion, this creates a sustainability question about future-year budgeting and may signal unmet demand in the baseline.
findings.figures: £575k non-recurring funding; 1,208 additional support hours; 10,927 hours recurring baseline allocation
findings.quote: The ASL Generic Support budget is currently projected to exceed its recurring budget allocation by £575k. This reflects the agreed use of non-recurring resources to enhance staffing support across the service. The additional funding is providing 1,208 hours of support in excess of the recurring allocation of 10,927 hours.

findings.committee: Education, Skills and Community Wellbeing Committee
findings.paper_title: ESCW Q1 Revenue Budget Monitoring 202627 Report
findings.headline: Consultation on nursery closures has been delayed, creating risk to agreed savings delivery
findings.detail: The council planned savings of £1,890k for the directorate, including a saving from consulting on closure of small nurseries. That consultation is delayed with no timetable given. The council states it has identified 'mitigating measures' but these are additional cost reductions, not the planned structural saving from closures.
findings.matters: Savings plans that slip early in the year signal delivery risk; if mitigation measures also slip, the council may need to find additional budget reductions mid-year.
findings.figures: £1,890k total agreed savings for the directorate; nursery closure saving not separately quantified; all other savings reported on track
findings.quote: There has been a delay in delivering the savings option relating to the consultation on the closure of small nurseries, with the consultation process for the identified nurseries currently being progressed. The Directorate has identified offsetting mitigating measures to address the delayed delivery of this saving.

findings.committee: Education, Skills and Community Wellbeing Committee
findings.paper_title: ESCW Q1 Revenue Budget Monitoring 202627 Report
findings.headline: First quarter £337k drawdown from Supporting Learners reserves to cover staffing pressures
findings.detail: The Supporting Learners budget is consuming £337k from agreed reserves in Q1 to support £575k of non-recurring resources for Additional Support for Learning staffing. This is driven by recruitment challenges and staffing vacancies elsewhere in the function, which generated only £238k in offsetting underspends.
findings.matters: Reserve drawdown in Q1 to cover staffing pressures signals reduced financial flexibility for managing unexpected in-year costs or slippage elsewhere.
findings.figures: £337k reserve drawdown; £575k non-recurring ASL commitment; £238k offsetting underspends; 1,208 additional support hours provided beyond 10,927 recurring allocation
findings.quote: a drawdown of £337k from the agreed reserve is currently anticipated. The position will continue to be closely monitored through regular budget monitoring meetings to ensure sufficient resources remain available to meet the needs of pupils.

findings.committee: Education, Skills and Community Wellbeing Committee
findings.paper_title: ESCW Q1 Revenue Budget Monitoring 202627 Appendix 1
findings.headline: Supporting Learners projects a £337k overspend in Q1, with ASL Generic Support exceeding budget by £575k
findings.detail: The Supporting Learners service is projected to spend £22,288k against a revised budget of £21,951k, an overspend of £337k. Within this, ASL Generic Support is forecast at £13,724k against a budget of £13,149k – a £575k overspend representing 4.4% of that line's budget. The council is applying the Supporting Learners Additionality Reserve to address this variance.
findings.matters: Supporting Learners is a demand-led statutory service where overspends are driven by pupil need rather than discretionary spending. A Q1 overspend of this magnitude in a service the council cannot refuse signals structural cost pressure. Drawing reserves to cover in-year spending pressures reduces financial resilience for future shocks.
findings.figures: Supporting Learners overspend £337k on budget £21,951k (1.5%); ASL Generic Support overspend £575k on budget £13,149k (4.4%); position as at 30 June 2026
findings.quote: Application of Supporting Learners Additionality Reserve (337)

findings.committee: Education, Skills and Community Wellbeing Committee
findings.paper_title: ESCW Q1 Revenue Budget Monitoring 202627 Appendix 2
findings.headline: Formal consultation on nursery closures is delaying £186k in planned savings
findings.detail: The paper states planned savings from nursery closures have been delayed pending completion of formal consultation. The council notes this shortfall has been offset through mitigating savings, but this shows consultation timing is creating schedule risk in the savings plan.
findings.matters: Savings delivery faces execution risks beyond budget decisions — administrative processes like consultations can delay planned cuts and force the council to find compensating savings elsewhere.
findings.figures: £186k delayed from consultation process
findings.quote: The planned saving has been delayed pending completion of the formal consultation process for the identified nurseries. The resulting shortfall has been fully offset through mitigating savings identified within this area.

findings.committee: Education, Skills and Community Wellbeing Committee
findings.paper_title: ESCW Q1 Revenue Budget Monitoring 202627 Appendix 2
findings.headline: £1,436k of £1,890k planned 2026/27 savings (76%) remain dependent on staffing exercises and service reviews not yet completed
findings.detail: The council has already achieved £454k in savings but the bulk of the plan remains subject to ongoing implementation. The largest single item (£656k from removing the permanent supply teacher pool) depends on a staffing exercise commencing in August 2026. Other material items including school technician centralization (£99k), community planning restructure (£40k), and nursery closure consultation (£186k) are similarly incomplete.
findings.matters: A finance director needs to track whether budget is built on confirmed actions or incomplete ones; a lender needs confidence that the council's savings plan will execute as scheduled and not slip.
findings.figures: Total 2026/27 savings target £1,890k; Already achieved £454k; Subject to ongoing review £1,436k; Supply teacher removal £656k; School technician centralization £99k; Nursery consultation £186k
findings.quote: A staffing exercise is currently being undertaken within the Directorate to implement the agreed plan and deliver the required saving.

findings.headline: Capital project over budget due to extension of time requiring active funder engagement.
findings.detail: Lockerbie Enterprise and Wellbeing Hub achieved practical completion in Q1 2026/27 but exceeded approved budget due to extension of time. Council is working with LOS (delivery partner) to address budget pressures with support from external funders. Facility expected to open to public Q2 2026/27.
findings.matters: A completed project exceeding budget with cost negotiations ongoing indicates cost control challenges and dependency on funder forbearance for project delivery.
findings.figures: Budget overage amount not disclosed
findings.quote: The project achieved practical completion Q1 2026/27, over budget due to extension of time, but work is being undertaken by LOS to address this with support from funders. DGC Officers continue to work with LOS to address budget pressures and manage the move from construction phase to operational.

findings.headline: Significant programme-wide reprofiling with council provisioning £4m for additional slippage anticipation.
findings.detail: £28.7m of major budget moves required: Whitesands accelerated £8.2m, Borderlands/Stranraer Marina deferred £15.5m to 2028/29, Dumfries Academy moved £2.2m to 2028/29, plus other adjustments. Council explicitly states the reprofiling value "is higher than would normally be the case at this point in the year" and has built in £4m contingency for further slippage, "recognising the significant capital programme and experience from recent years".
findings.matters: Extent of mid-year reprofiling combined with explicit budgeting for further slippage signals structural programme delivery challenges and management's expectation of continued delays.
findings.figures: £8.2m (Whitesands), £15.5m (Borderlands), £2.2m (Dumfries Academy), £4m (further slippage allowance)
findings.quote: The value of reprofiling required in 2026/27, primarily due to the changes in the Whitesands and Stranraer Marina spending plans is higher than would normally be the case at this point in the year... An allowance of £4M for further slippage in the programme (recognising the significant capital programme and experience from recent years)

findings.headline: Grant-funded transport project faces compliance breach: LUF cycle improvements had construction work refused listed building consent, creating grant funding agreement risk.
findings.detail: Kier, Penpont and Tynron Development Trust (KPTDT) completed ~80% of the Penpont-Thornhill active travel path but listed building consent application for cycle/pedestrian bridge works was refused. The objection centred on a pedestrian barrier not in keeping with the listed structure. Council legal services are now engaged in dialogue with KPTDT to ensure compliance with grant funding agreement terms; impact on project programme and cost to be assessed.
findings.matters: A £878,482 Levelling Up grant faces non-compliance risk due to completed construction work that failed listed building consent. This creates real exposure to grant clawback and requires remediation, affecting both cost and programme.
findings.figures: £878,482 (Levelling Up funds at risk)
findings.quote: Whilst full planning permission was granted for works completed to provide safe passage over the Nith bridge for cyclists and pedestrians, an application for listed building consent to cover the works completed to the listed structure of the bridge was refused. Feedback centred on a pedestrian barrier which objectors felt was not in keeping with the listed structure... Work is ongoing with legal services to commence dialogue with the group to ensure compliance with the terms of the grant funding agreement KPTDT entered with the Council which will provide up to £878,482 of Levelling up funds upon completion of the project.

findings.headline: Major school project contractor withdrawal with 2+ year delay: Morgan Sindall withdrew from Dumfries Academy refurbishment; replacement contractor extends completion to late 2029/early 2030.
findings.detail: Morgan Sindall, the Tier One contractor, confirmed in April 2026 it would not proceed with the Academy refurbishment and Loreburn Primary relocation. Morrison Construction was appointed June 2026 as replacement. Construction now scheduled to commence end of 2027 with completion expected late 2029 or early 2030, representing a substantial programme extension from the original schedule.
findings.matters: Contractor withdrawal from a major school infrastructure project and resulting 2+ year delay signals delivery execution risk and potential cost implications on a significant capital asset.
findings.figures: No specific cost impact disclosed
findings.quote: Hub South West's Tier One contractor, Morgan Sindall, confirmed in April 2026 that it no longer wished to proceed with the refurbishment of the Academy and the relocation of Loreburn Primary School. Following an interview process on 3 June 2026, Morrison Construction Scotland (MCS) was formally appointed by Hub South West as the replacement contractor... anticipated that construction works will commence towards the end of 2027, with completion expected in late 2029 or early 2030.

findings.headline: Agreed 2026/27 savings targets not being achieved, with shortfalls requiring Corporate Change Fund funding
findings.detail: The report notes 'there are projected shortfalls against the delivery of a small number of savings in the current year'. Rather than achieving the agreed £1.234m in savings (including carryforwards from 2025/26), the council is relying on the Corporate Change Fund to cover 'shortfalls that were brought forward from 2025/26'. This indicates savings planned in the budget are not being realised.
findings.matters: Budget is dependent on unachieved savings; creates structural pressure requiring ongoing central funding support.
findings.figures: £1.234 million in agreed savings; portion in shortfall requiring Corporate Change Fund mitigation
findings.quote: there are projected shortfalls against the delivery of a small number of savings in the current year. While ongoing efforts to reduce and address these shortfalls will continue, it is currently projected that these will require to be funded in-year through the Corporate Change Fund.

findings.headline: Aging council fleet generating £90k maintenance pressure and cascading vehicle hire costs across multiple services
findings.detail: Fleet Management is forecast to show a £90k pressure. 'Costs associated with repairing and maintaining the Council's ageing fleet of vehicles have resulted in budget pressures in prior years, with a pressure of £90k forecast for 2026/27. This has also directly impacted other services in terms of additional costs being incurred for vehicle hire to ensure service delivery.' A Fleet Board review is underway but 'will be reported back to Members as further information becomes available', with no timeline given.
findings.matters: Aging asset base creating cascading cost impact across multiple services; no clear capital replacement plan evident.
findings.figures: £90k fleet pressure; vehicle hire costs impacting Neighbourhood Services (£262k overspend includes vehicle hire component)
findings.quote: Costs associated with repairing and maintaining the Council's ageing fleet of vehicles have resulted in budget pressures in prior years, with a pressure of £90k forecast for 2026/27. This has also directly impacted other services in terms of additional costs being incurred for vehicle hire to ensure service delivery.

findings.headline: Neighbourhood Services experiencing £262k overspend with ongoing pressures in vehicle hire, contract work and income recovery
findings.detail: Neighbourhood Services is forecast to return a £262k overspend. 'The main areas of pressure the service experienced in the previous financial year, including vehicle hire, payments to external sub-contractors associated with tree works and burials income are expected to continue in 2026/27.' A service review is currently underway but no resolution timeline is given. The council removed a planned £55k income uprating from burials 'recognising the challenges in achieving this income target'.
findings.matters: Recurring pressures from prior year showing no resolution; income target adjustment signals planned income is unachievable.
findings.figures: £262k overspend; £55k burials income uprating removed
findings.quote: The main areas of pressure the service experienced in the previous financial year, including vehicle hire, payments to external sub-contractors associated with tree works and burials income are expected to continue in 2026/27.

findings.headline: School transport facing combined £600k pressure with procurement compliance issues in mainstream transport
findings.detail: ASN (Additional Support Needs) home-to-school transport is forecast at £360k pressure 'due to increased eligibility and higher price increases from service providers'. Mainstream under-16 seater transport shows £240k pressure 'due to price increases and non-contract spend'. The report notes work is underway 'to increase the level of procurement compliance within this area, and secure cost efficiencies', indicating current spend is not fully controlled.
findings.matters: Two related services both experiencing significant cost growth; procurement compliance issues suggest poor cost control and further risk of overspend.
findings.figures: ASN transport £360k pressure; mainstream transport £240k pressure; both subject to change based on 'transport requirements for the new academic year in August 2026'
findings.quote: Pressures on home to school transport for ASN children are expected to continue in 2026/27 due to increased eligibility and higher price increases from service providers. This pressure is currently forecast at £360k.

findings.headline: Waste Services facing £600k recurring cost pressure with reliance on non-recurring EPR funding to balance
findings.detail: Waste Services is forecast to return a £600k overspend driven by: increase in waste diversion costs, reduction in recyclate income, increase in waste disposal costs from Scottish Environment Protection Agency changes, and significant contract price increases for waste treatment. The council plans to fund this through 'non-recurring EPR funding to address existing pressures'. The new Dumfries Zero Waste Park opening later in 2026/27 has 'costs associated with the running of this facility are still being evaluated'.
findings.matters: Waste is showing persistent operational losses being covered by one-off funding; new facility adds further unquantified cost risk mid-year.
findings.figures: £600k overspend forecast; costs of Zero Waste Park 'still being evaluated'
findings.quote: These pressures, as previously reported to Members, include an increase in waste diversion costs, a reduction in income from recyclates, and an increase in waste disposal costs resulting from changes imposed by the Scottish Environment Protection Agency. The service is also anticipating significant contract price increases relating to the treatment of waste.

findings.headline: £671k overspend forecast in Economy and Infrastructure directorate being absorbed through non-recurring funding sources
findings.detail: The directorate is currently projected to return a £671k overspend at the end of 2026/27 based on Q1 position. This is being mitigated through non-recurring sources including EPR funding in Waste Services (£600k of the overspend) and reserves in Property, Estates and Programmes. The report notes 'there are risks that this projected overspend could be further increased and close monitoring and associated mitigation measures will be required'.
findings.matters: The council is funding structural operational deficits through one-off resources rather than solving underlying cost problems, creating sustainability risk.
findings.figures: £671k overspend; £600k Waste Services pressure; £745k Transport and Infrastructure overspend; £262k Neighbourhood Services overspend
findings.quote: currently estimated that Economy and Infrastructure will return a £671k over budget position at the end of the financial year following the application of recurring and non-recurring funding sources

findings.headline: Cost control measures are creating system-wide pressures including NHS patient flow delays, triggering need for Scottish Government engagement
findings.detail: The aggressive care package management process intended to control costs has introduced operational and system pressures, including NHS patient flow and delayed discharge issues. The IJB, NHS and Scottish Government are now in collaborative discussions to address this, indicating the local solution is creating wider health system problems.
findings.matters: This indicates the cost-cutting measures may be unsustainable or require system-level intervention beyond the Council's control. If the Scottish Government imposes different requirements, it could undermine the financial recovery plan.
findings.figures: No specific figures; NHS delayed discharge and patient flow pressures noted
findings.quote: This approach has delivered savings but has also introduced operational pressures and wider system pressures, including NHS patient flow and delayed discharges, which have been adversely affected by the current care package management process

findings.headline: Slower-than-expected delivery of planned savings threatens ability to reach even the £4.5m forecast position
findings.detail: The financial recovery plan assumed faster and larger savings delivery. Even the £1.109m in additional anticipated savings is conditional on current recycling levels continuing. The report notes 'delivery of planned savings has been slower than originally assumed within the financial recovery plan.' The Council's own £2.8m recovery funding carries £1.9m still uncommitted, suggesting uncertainty about what will work.
findings.matters: If the planned savings trajectory cannot be maintained, the overspend will exceed the £4.5m forecast. The Council is already dependent on discretionary funding just to reach that position, and £1.9m of that fund remains without identified use.
findings.figures: Anticipated additional savings £1.109m; £1.9m of £2.8m recovery funding uncommitted; earlier opening pressure of £7.6m only reduced by £2m
findings.quote: While further savings are expected through care package recycling and other recovery measures, delivery has been slower than originally assumed. Continued action will therefore be required throughout the remainder of 2026/27 to achieve financial balance.

findings.headline: Physical Disability services facing £2.074m overspend with new high-cost packages offsetting recycling efforts and high-cost agency placements in place
findings.detail: Care package recycling is delivering some reductions, but new high-cost packages for new clients are creating an overall increase in care hours. Several high-cost agency-provided packages remain in place. The service expected cost reductions of around £500k but has not achieved them, and now requires external benchmarking to identify service redesign opportunities.
findings.matters: This shows a service losing control of cost growth: existing savings are being swallowed by new demand, and the council is unable to identify where cost control should focus without external help.
findings.figures: £2.074m overspend; expected cost reductions £500k not delivered; multiple high-cost agency packages remain
findings.quote: While some reductions have been achieved through the recycling of care packages, there have been new additional high cost packages put in place for new clients resulting in an overall increase in hours of care being delivered

findings.headline: Mental Health residential placements have tripled from 14 to 42 since 2023/24, driving £1.297m overspend
findings.detail: The number of Mental Health residential placements has grown significantly over recent years with no signs of stabilisation. This increased activity is the primary driver of the forecast budget pressure in this service. The service is only now beginning to review all residential placements to understand the increase.
findings.matters: This sharp, unexplained growth in a high-cost category (residential care) indicates either uncontrolled demand growth or previous under-budgeting. Either scenario represents a structural risk that cannot be addressed through short-term savings.
findings.figures: Placements increased from 14 (2023/24 average) to 42 (current); forecast overspend £1.297m
findings.quote: The number of Mental Health residential placements has increased significantly over recent years, rising from an average of 14 placements during 2023/24 to 42 placements currently. This increase in activity is the primary driver of the forecast budget pressure

findings.headline: Learning Disability services overspending by £4.854m with delivery of planned savings running 65% below target
findings.detail: Learning Disability is now the largest budget pressure. Through the first 12 weeks of the financial year, care at home hours reduced by only 176 hours per week against a planned reduction of around 500 hours. The report notes 'the service is attempting to control this against a significant increasing need.' Direct Payments savings have not yet materialised.
findings.matters: This single service area accounts for over 86% of the remaining £4.5m overspend. Failure to control LD costs poses an acute financial risk, as the underlying demand appears to be outpacing the council's ability to manage it.
findings.figures: £4.854m overspend; actual recycling 176 hours per week vs planned ~500 hours per week
findings.quote: Learning Disability services are currently projected to return an overspend of £4.854 million this financial year, with the overspend currently spread across all elements of care

findings.headline: Forecast £5.6m overspend on delegated social work budget with £4.5m remaining after planned savings
findings.detail: The revised opening projected overspend of £7.6m has improved to £5.6m at Q1, but recovery measures have delivered slower than expected. Even with anticipated further savings of £1.109m from care package recycling, a £4.5m overspend is forecast for year-end. The report explicitly states 'further measures will be required to achieve a balanced outturn position.'
findings.matters: This represents a direct financial risk to the Council. Under the Integration Scheme, the IJB would seek additional payment from the Council where there is an overspend, meaning the council may need to inject additional funds to cover delegated services.
findings.figures: Opening overspend £7.6m; Q1 overspend £5.6m; post-savings forecast £4.5m; anticipated savings £1.109m; £2.8m recovery funding provided by Council
findings.quote: While responsibility for decision making, and budgetary control, for delegated services is the responsibility of the IJB, this forecast position represents a significant financial risk to the Council

findings.headline: Adult social care services experience sustained demand, increasing complexity of needs, and inflation in provider costs that cannot be fully offset.
findings.detail: The paper emphasises that services experienced "sustained demand for adult social care services, increasing complexity of care needs and the ongoing impact of inflation on the provision of commissioned services". These pressures have a statutory nature with limited alternatives to meet assessed need, meaning the council cannot unilaterally reduce services to balance budgets.
findings.matters: Demand-driven pressures outside management control due to statutory obligations indicate structural budget risk that could require additional council funding in future years.
findings.figures: Services across Physical Disability (£2.643m), Older People (£812k), Learning Disability (£5.567m) and Mental Health (£2.219m) all experienced sustained demand
findings.quote: The final outturn position reflects sustained demand for adult social care services, increasing complexity of care needs and the ongoing impact of inflation on the provision of commissioned services

findings.headline: Learning Disability Services overspent by £5.567m with structural budget challenges and deteriorating position since Q3.
findings.detail: Learning Disability Services represents the largest service pressure within the delegated budget at £5.567m, deteriorating by £245k since Q3. The service experiences structural budget challenges because a small number of service users require very high support levels, creating inherent expenditure volatility and unpredictability.
findings.matters: As the largest single service pressure with structural causes, this indicates major service transformation is needed, not minor adjustments.
findings.figures: Learning Disability £5.567m overspend; deterioration of £245k since Q3; one additional high-cost care package commissioned during the year
findings.quote: Learning Disability Services reported an overspend of £5.567m, representing the largest service pressure within the delegated budget and a deterioration of £245k since Quarter 3

findings.headline: £7.02m projected budget gap for 2026/27 with a Financial Recovery Plan that carries significant delivery risks.
findings.detail: The IJB faces a £7.02m projected budget gap for 2026/27 and has approved a Financial Recovery Plan to address it. The paper explicitly states the recovery plan contains "significant risks relating to non-delivery of savings and the need to move to financially sustainable care models". The council has allocated £2.8m within its budget to support delivery, but outcome is not assured.
findings.matters: This is a structural recurring deficit with explicit execution risks in the recovery plan, indicating ongoing budget vulnerability.
findings.figures: £7.02m projected budget gap for 2026/27; £2.8m council allowance to support recovery plan; delegated budget of £124.25m
findings.quote: The financial recovery plan contains significant risks relating to non-delivery of savings and the need to move to financially sustainable care models

findings.headline: £9.498m overspend on delegated adult social care services required additional council funding.
findings.detail: The Integration Joint Board's delegated adult social care services overspent by £9.498m in 2025/26, representing 8.9% of the delegated budget. The council approved additional funding to cover this deficit at its Enabling and Customer Services Committee on 16 June 2026. The overspend was driven by demand-led expenditure across Physical Disability, Learning Disability and Mental Health services.
findings.matters: A material deficit requiring additional council funding represents structural financial risk and diverts resources from other council priorities.
findings.figures: £9.498m overspend on £107.019m delegated budget (8.9%); Learning Disability £5.567m, Physical Disability £2.643m, Mental Health £2.219m
findings.quote: that there was an overspend of £9.498m for services delegated to the Integration Joint Board for the financial year 2025/26 as reflected in the Appendix

findings.headline: Service reductions are proving difficult to implement against critical need assessments
findings.detail: Several planned reductions in care at home and direct payments are not being achieved as assumed. The paper notes services are "assess[ing] for critical need and allocate budget based on recycling allowances," suggesting capacity constraints and difficulty in withdrawing support. Learning Disability Care at Home is tracking at only 51% of plan (£738k of £1,438k); Older People Reablement only 24% (£143k of £590k).
findings.matters: This suggests either a rise in demand for critical-need services or inability to implement planned reductions; both indicate service pressure and potential overspend risk if the IJB cannot control care costs.
findings.figures: Learning Disability Care at Home: planned -1,438k, expected -738k (51%); Older People Reablement Model: planned -590k, expected -143k (24%)
findings.quote: The service continue to assess for critical need and allocate budget based on recycling allowances

findings.headline: Major social care transformation initiatives have not started or are severely delayed
findings.detail: Three substantial planned savings initiatives are either not progressing or very early-stage: Learning Disability Technology (only £23k of £632k planned, 4%); Social Care Visioning (£0 of £1,178k, still in partnership development); and Responder Service (£0 of £150k, alternatives still being explored). Supported Housing Development reports delays with full access "available later in the year."
findings.matters: If these initiatives do not materialise, the savings gap widens further; they represent over £2m of the planned £7m, so their failure would make the shortfall catastrophic.
findings.figures: Learning Disability Technology: planned -632k, expected -23k; Social Care Visioning: planned -1,178k, expected £0; Responder Service: planned -150k, expected £0
findings.quote: Public sector partnership is currently being developed, it is too early to determine what savings will come from care avoidance at this point in time.

findings.headline: £4.76m shortfall in planned social care savings threatens IJB budget
findings.detail: The IJB agreed £7,020k in savings targets for 2026/27 but currently expects to deliver only £2,256k by year-end. This leaves £4,764k (68%) of planned savings unachieved. By Q1, only £1,147k (16%) had been realised, and multiple initiatives show minimal progress.
findings.matters: Social care is a major cost area for councils and their IJB partners; undelivered savings of this scale will likely force budget pressures onto the council's main budget, potentially requiring reserve drawdowns or further cost control measures.
findings.figures: Agreed Savings Plan 2026/27: £7,020k; Savings achieved to 30 June: £1,147k; Current expected total delivery 2026/27: £2,256k; Shortfall: £4,764k
findings.quote: Currernt Expected Savings to be delivered in 2026/27 - 2,256 [against] Agreed Savings Plan 2026/27 - 7,020

findings.headline: Budget balance achieved through staff vacancies and turnover, not service improvement
findings.detail: Overspendings in placements and accommodation have been 'offset by staff vacancies, turn over' and 'mitigated through vacant positions and staff turnover.' These are presented as mitigation mechanisms, not solutions.
findings.matters: Using vacancies to balance budgets is not sustainable. Suggests staffing below establishment and may affect service continuity and quality going forward.
findings.figures: £1.086M + £324k overspends offset by vacancy management
findings.quote: which have been offset by staff vacancies, turn over and additional investment measure funding

findings.headline: Residential and family placement pressures described as certain to continue into 2026/27
findings.detail: Report explicitly states residential placement pressure 'is likely to continue into the new financial year 2026/27 and will be subject to close monitoring and a key focus for the Management Team.' Similar forward warning for temporary accommodation.
findings.matters: Council is flagging these as structural, ongoing budget challenges, not one-offs. Matters for projecting 2026/27 budget risk.
findings.figures: £1.086M residential overspend + £324k family placements = £1.41M ongoing pressure
findings.quote: This pressure is likely to continue into the new financial year 2026/27 and will be subject to close monitoring and a key focus for the Management Team.

findings.headline: Family placement allowances overspend £324k due to inability to recruit in-house foster carers
findings.detail: High-cost external placements are being used because of recruitment failures. Additional investment funding available for this purpose cannot be deployed due to inability to recruit intensive foster carers.
findings.matters: Shows inability to deliver core provision in-house, forcing reliance on expensive external market. Signals workforce or pay challenges that may affect other services.
findings.figures: £324k overspend in family placement allowances
findings.quote: Family placement allowances returned an overspend of £324k, associated with the ongoing challenges to recruit foster carers resulting in the need to use high-cost external placements.

findings.paper_title: SWS Q4 Budget Monitoring Report SWS_
findings.headline: Children Residential Placements overspend £1.086M with average cost per placement rising above budget
findings.detail: Budget was enhanced to £8.848M but expenditure reached £9.934M. The number of placements fell from 32 to 28, but average cost per placement has continued to increase beyond budget, creating the core pressure.
findings.matters: Cost inflation that persists despite volume reduction indicates underlying service cost growth not under control, signalling structural rather than cyclical pressure.
findings.figures: £8.848M budget vs £9.934M expenditure; placements 32 → 28; overspend reduced by only £82k from Q3

findings.headline: Early Learning and Childcare place uptake is lower than anticipated
findings.detail: ELC service underspent by £557k, with the report attributing this to 'lower‑than‑anticipated uptake of ELC places during the year, which meant that recruitment to the projected staffing establishment was not required.' This indicates actual demand for council-funded ELC places fell below planning assumptions.
findings.matters: Lower than expected uptake of funded childcare places suggests demand assumptions may not be holding, which could reflect demographic trends or policy take-up issues affecting the council's forward planning and staffing.
findings.figures: £557k underspend; lower-than-anticipated ELC place uptake

findings.committee: Education, Skills and Community Wellbeing Committee
findings.paper_title: Education, Skills & Community Wellbeing Revenue Budget Outturn 202526 Report
findings.headline: Additional Support for Learners spending is £656k above budget and flagged as an ongoing pressure into 2026/27
findings.detail: The ASL Generic Support budget exceeded budget by £656k to meet actual pupil support needs in schools. The council originally planned to draw reserves to cover this overspend. While the directorate-wide underspend meant reserves were not drawn this year, the report explicitly notes this 'will continue to be an area of focus for 2026/27 with updates to be provided through the new year's monitoring cycle', indicating the demand pressure is expected to persist.
findings.matters: Rising demand for additional pupil support is outpacing budget assumptions and is flagged by the council as an continuing issue requiring focus, creating risk of ongoing budget pressures and possible reserve drawdown in future years.
findings.figures: £656k above budgeted expenditure in ASL Generic Support; overall ASL overspend £51k
findings.quote: the ASL Generic Support budget incurred expenditure of £656k above the budgeted level in order to meet the additional support needs of pupils across Schools. This will continue to be an area of focus for 2026/27 with updates to be provided through the new year's monitoring cycle.

findings.headline: Multiple income streams are underperforming and demand-driven, creating budget forecasting challenges
findings.detail: Three separate income sources underperformed in 2025/26: licensing income (liquor, gambling, civic) was under budget due to fluctuating demand and a continuing reduction in liquor premises; Registrar income under-recovered due to a decrease in civil marriage ceremonies; and Organisational Development failed to achieve budgeted income from external training placements. All three are flagged for ongoing monitoring in 2026/27.
findings.matters: Income volatility and declining demand in multiple areas makes budget forecasting less reliable and exposes the council to recurring revenue shortfalls. The trend in civil marriages and licensed premises suggests structural decline rather than temporary fluctuations.
findings.figures: Registrar income underperformance in Customer and Digital's £190k underspend; licensing income pressure within Governance and Human Resources
findings.quote: Registrar income, within Customer Services, under recovered against the budgeted target due to a decrease in civil marriage ceremonies. This was partially offset by staffing vacancies and staff retention during the year. Due to Registrar income being demand led, and thus subject to fluctuations, this area will also be a primary focus of budget monitoring in 2026/27.

findings.headline: Legal Services recruitment and retention challenges are being managed through costly external legal expertise
findings.detail: Legal Services faced recruitment and retention challenges in filling professional solicitor roles during 2025/26. The service has managed staffing shortfalls by using external legal expertise, which is described as costly. The service plans to address this by developing trainee solicitors with the intention of reducing the need for external support, but progress will be subject to ongoing review.
findings.matters: Reliance on external legal expertise is a temporary and costly workaround that increases expenditure. If recruitment and retention challenges persist, the council faces either ongoing higher legal costs or service delivery delays.
findings.figures: Governance and Human Resources underspend of £103k, partly offset by external legal expertise costs
findings.quote: Legal Services faced recruitment and retention challenges in filling professional roles during the financial year, predominantly solicitor roles. As a result, staffing shortfalls have been managed, where appropriate, using external legal expertise.

findings.headline: Revenue and Benefits service cannot reduce staffing despite a reduction in the Housing Benefit Admin Subsidy grant
findings.detail: The Revenue and Benefits service faces a structural mismatch: grant funding has been reduced, but the service faces continued high demand for welfare and benefits support. The service has been unable to reduce staffing levels to match the reduced grant due to high volumes of applications for Council Tax Reduction and Scottish Welfare Fund. Additionally, postal and bank charges exceeded budget.
findings.matters: This indicates a demand-led cost pressure that is not controllable through staffing decisions. If demand continues to outpace grant funding in 2026/27, the directorate will face an ongoing budget pressure that may force a choice between service quality and cost control.
findings.figures: Revenue and Benefits service overspend of £21k contributed to Finance and Procurement's £21k overspend
findings.quote: The service has been unable to reduce staffing levels to match a reduction in the Housing Benefit Admin Subsidy grant due to continued high volumes of applications for Council Tax Reduction and Scottish Welfare Fund.

findings.headline: Agreed savings of £800k not delivered on schedule; £153k drawn from Change Fund
findings.detail: The directorate was responsible for delivering £1.140m in agreed savings for 2025/26. Whilst £340k was achieved at the outset, the remaining £800k required ongoing monitoring throughout the year. Due to timing delays in delivery, a non-recurring contribution of £153k from the Change Fund was required to close the gap, though the savings are expected to be achieved in full in 2026/27.
findings.matters: Lenders care whether a council can deliver committed savings on schedule. This suggests the directorate is struggling with the pace of implementation, creating a pattern of delay and reliance on non-recurring support.
findings.figures: £800k savings delayed; £153k Change Fund draw; £1.140m total savings responsibility; £340k achieved on schedule
findings.quote: The appendix highlights that a non-recurring contribution of £153k from the Change Fund was required due to timing delays in delivery.

findings.headline: Core financial position dependent on £2M one-off ePER waste funding and £1.303M energy savings partly from Ice Bowl closure
findings.detail: The £6.489M corporate surplus includes £2M Extended Producer Responsibility funding explicitly flagged as 'one-off basis' and £1.303M energy savings partly from 'closure of the Ice Bowl'. Without these non-recurring items, underlying variances would be £3.5M weaker.
findings.matters: The council's apparent financial flexibility is partly non-recurring. The underlying recurring position is weaker, making future years more challenging if these variances do not repeat.
findings.figures: ePER funding £2M (one-off); Energy savings £1.303M (includes asset closure)
findings.quote: it has been possible to release £2 Million of this income to support the Council's wider pressures on a one-off basis.

findings.headline: Home to school transport for children with additional support needs overran by £320k despite £500k additional budget allocation
findings.detail: The service received £500k additional budget pressure funding during the year but still finished £320k over budget. The paper flags this requires 'further work' and 'opportunities to improve budgetary control' in 2026/27.
findings.matters: Service demand or unit costs are not responding to additional investment, signalling either structural cost inflation or scope creep that additional money does not resolve.
findings.figures: £500k additional allocation; £320k final overspend
findings.quote: The extent of overspending on Home to School Transport for children with additional support needs was reduced to £320k following the allocation of additional budget pressure funding of £500k

findings.headline: Only 83% of agreed 2025/26 savings delivered, with £662k shortfall covered from reserves
findings.detail: The council achieved 83% of its planned savings target, with the £662k shortfall funded from the Change Fund. This continuation of underdelivery signals execution risk on future savings programmes.
findings.matters: Inability to deliver planned savings forces councils into deeper reserve drawdown or unplanned service cuts. This pattern of miss signals capability constraints.
findings.figures: 83% delivery rate; £662k shortfall
findings.quote: while 83% of the savings target has been delivered, a shortfall in the delivery of agreed savings has required a contribution of £662k from the Change Fund, in line with the agreed approach.

findings.headline: Children's residential placements still £1.1M over budget despite headcount reduction from 32 to 28
findings.detail: The council reduced placements during the year but spending remained £1.1M over budget. The paper flags this will require 'ongoing active management' in 2026/27, indicating the underlying unit costs are not sustainable at current levels.
findings.matters: Service inflation is outpacing budget growth; reducing headcount has not brought spending into line, suggesting a recurring structural pressure.
findings.figures: Placements reduced from 32 to 28; £1.1M overspend persists
findings.quote: the overall expenditure incurred in supporting children's residential placements was still £1.1 Million over the budgeted level and will continue to require ongoing active management and monitoring over the upcoming financial year

findings.headline: Integration Joint Board overspend of £9.497M being funded as non-recoverable contribution from reserves
findings.detail: The IJB (health & social care board) overran by £9.497M, with main pressure in care for under-65s with complex needs. The council is covering this through £6.489M corporate variances and £3.022M reserve release. For 2026/27, the IJB has agreed a Change & Savings Plan to balance within budget, indicating this is a structural recurring issue.
findings.matters: A material unplanned cost (2% of council budget) is being absorbed from reserves rather than from operational improvement, and the IJB's need for a corrective plan signals the pressure will recur.
findings.figures: £9.497M overspend; £6.489M corporate variances; £3.022M from reserves
findings.quote: the extent of year end overspending remained significant at £9.497 Million, with the main areas of pressure continuing to be experienced in relation to the provision of care and support to individuals under 65 years of age with complex care needs.

findings.headline: Council anticipates no significant cash reserves due to capital borrowing commitments
findings.detail: The council does not expect to hold significant cash balances above day-to-day operational needs because of the large borrowing requirements for the capital programme. This limits the council's ability to generate investment income and leaves minimal financial headroom.
findings.matters: Limited cash reserves reduce the council's financial flexibility and resilience to unexpected costs or revenue shocks, and eliminate diversified revenue sources from treasury investments.
findings.figures: None
findings.quote: Given the significant borrowing requirements over the upcoming period, we do not anticipate holding any significant cash balances over and above that required for day-to-day cash management, therefore the potential to generate any significant investment interest will be limited over the upcoming period.

findings.headline: £75 million external funding for flood protection and marina schemes is unlocked by the council increasing its own borrowing contribution
findings.detail: Full Council on 11 December 2025 agreed to increase the council's contribution to the Whitesands Flood Protection Scheme and Stranraer Marina to allow the release of £75 million in external funding. However, this decision increased the council's own borrowing requirement as reflected in the updated treasury strategy.
findings.matters: This demonstrates the council's reliance on external funding partners for major capital schemes and its willingness to increase debt to unlock external resources, which affects overall leverage and debt sustainability.
findings.figures: £75 Million external funding released; council contribution increased (amount unspecified)
findings.quote: Full Council on 11 December 2025 agreed to increase the Council contribution to the Whitesands Flood Protection Scheme and Stranraer Marina to allow the release of £75 Million external funding and progress these important projects for our region. However, this did increase the Council's borrowing requirement as reflected in the 2026/27 Treasury Strategy.

findings.headline: Treasury borrowing limits may need updating if interest rate reductions slow from forecast
findings.detail: The council acknowledges that short-term borrowing repayments approaching the under-12-months, 12-24-months, and 2-5-year treasury limits requires close ongoing monitoring. If interest rate reductions pace slows, updates to these limits may be brought to members.
findings.matters: Treasury limits are a key governance control and credit constraint; updating them signals the council's debt profile risk has changed, which would be material to lenders assessing refinancing capacity.
findings.figures: Limits in under 12 months, 12 months to 2 years, 2-to-5-year categories
findings.quote: There is no immediate need to alter these limits, however, the adequacy of these limits continues to be closely monitored, along with borrowing rate forecasts. Should any updates to these limits be required, a report will be brought forward to Members at the appropriate time, particularly if the pace of interest rate reductions slows from current forecasts.

findings.headline: Short-term borrowing strategy creates refinancing risk if interest rates do not fall as forecast
findings.detail: The council is prioritising 1-5 year borrowing initially while rates are expected to fall, but also needs some longer-dated 10+ year borrowing to protect against refinancing risk. The focus on shorter-term borrowing will result in higher repayment percentages falling due in the 1-5 year categories, closer to existing treasury limits.
findings.matters: If interest rate forecasts prove wrong or rates rise unexpectedly, the council faces material refinancing costs and potential pressure on treasury limits, reducing financial flexibility.
findings.figures: 1 to 5 years borrowing will be prioritised; some 10 year+ borrowing also needed
findings.quote: It is anticipated that relatively short term (1 to 5 years) borrowing will be utilised first given the indication that interest rates are due to fall back over the next two years. However, given the significant borrowing requirement over the upcoming period and to protect the Council from refinancing risk, some longer dated 10 year+ borrowing will also need to be undertaken.

findings.headline: Council has a £169 million borrowing requirement over the next three years
findings.detail: The borrowing is needed to support a 10-year capital investment strategy agreed in February 2026, including the new Dumfries High School, Roads Investment, and Dumfries Zero Waste Park. The revenue budget for 2026/27 to 2027/28 has been updated to include additional loan charge contributions to ensure this borrowing is affordable and sustainable.
findings.matters: This scale of capital investment and associated debt directly impacts the council's long-term financial sustainability and revenue capacity for other services.
findings.figures: £169 Million over the next 3 years
findings.quote: As outlined at Section 3 of the Strategy, based on the updated 2026/27 to 2035/36 Capital Investment Strategy, the Council has a borrowing requirement of £169 Million over the next 3 years.

findings.headline: Council must achieve recurring budget balance without using non-recurring reserves
findings.detail: Budget proposals are explicitly directed to avoid the use of non-recurring reserves as part of balancing the Council's recurring budgeted spend for the upcoming period. This represents a tightening of previous practice and removes a historical flexibility.
findings.matters: This hardening of discipline signals the council recognises it cannot sustain reserve drawdowns indefinitely; it is forcing structural solutions, not accounting treatments.
findings.figures: No reserve balance figures disclosed in this report
findings.quote: Avoid the use of non-recurring reserves as part of balancing the Council's recurring budgeted spend for the upcoming period

findings.headline: Scottish Government budget signals cash flat funding for 2027/28 and 2028/29, intensifying future years' funding pressure
findings.detail: The Scottish Budget includes cash flat (no real increase) revenue funding settlements for local government for 2027/28 and 2028/29. While subject to parliamentary scrutiny, the report notes these are 'very high level figures' and emphasises the importance of achieving a recurring budget balance in 2026/27.
findings.matters: Cash flat settlements mean no real-terms grant increase whilst costs inflate with pay awards and demand; this locks in a structural deficit position that will persist unless savings are sustained or council tax rises sharply.
findings.figures: Cash flat (no percentage increase specified)
findings.quote: The Scottish Budget includes very high level figures that reflects cash flat revenue funding settlements for local government for 2027/28 and 2028/29. While the Scottish Government has indicated that these figures will be subject to change, it is apparent that this is likely to result in extremely tight funding settlements for local government in future years

findings.headline: Council capped from further capital investment due to loan charges from recent borrowing; Kirkcudbright Bridge replacement named as unavoidable future commitment
findings.detail: Members are advised to avoid any further capital investment and associated borrowing over the next period. The report cites 'loan charges implications of the increases in capital investment and associated borrowing agreed by Full Council in December 2025' and identifies the Kirkcudbright Bridge replacement as an unavoidable future requirement.
findings.matters: Restrictions on new capital borrowing indicate the council is at or near prudential borrowing headroom; existing commitments (notably bridge replacement) will consume future capital resources.
findings.figures: Specific amounts not disclosed; Kirkcudbright Bridge replacement is named as unavoidable
findings.quote: need for future funding of unavoidable requirements such as the Kirkcudbright Bridge replacement, Members are advised to seek to avoid any further additional investment and associated borrowing over the upcoming period at this stage

findings.headline: Council must deliver £8.7 million in savings for 2026/27, escalating to £24.9 million by 2028/29
findings.detail: The council has identified net savings options totalling £8.678 Million for 2026/27, increasing to £24.933 Million by 2028/29. These are essential options to address the funding gap. Savings include measures carried forward from 2025/26 and operational options subject to public consultation.
findings.matters: Failure to deliver savings of this magnitude would leave the council in budget crisis; this represents significant execution risk and service delivery risk.
findings.figures: £8.678 Million for 2026/27; £24.933 Million by 2028/29
findings.quote: Details of net savings options totalling £8.678 Million for 2026/27, increasing up to £24.933 Million by 2028/29 have been provided to Members, which can be reflected within group budget proposals to reduce the projected funding gap

findings.headline: Council to subsidise Integrated Joint Board health and social care by £2.5–3 million for 'change and savings plan'
findings.detail: The IJB (health and social care partnership) is presenting a 'Change and Savings Plan' to Council on 24 March 2026. The council is advised to make provision of around £2.5–3 Million in its 2026/27 budget to support this plan. Additionally, £5.558 Million in Scottish Government funding for adult social care wage increases and free nursing care is to be passed to the IJB.
findings.matters: Health and social care overspends are a recurring drag on council finances; a plan requiring a subsidy signals ongoing cost control difficulties in this area.
findings.figures: £2.5–3 Million provision recommended; £5.558 Million additional Scottish Government funding for social care
findings.quote: provision of around £2.5 - £3 Million might be considered appropriate for this purpose. If additional provision is made within the Council's agreed budget for this purpose, the release of any additional funding to support the IJB would be subject to further Member consideration through Full Council based on a clear change and savings plan that sets out how the IJB will return to containing spending within agreed budget levels on a sustainable basis

findings.headline: Council faces a £34.8 million structural funding gap across three years (2026/27 to 2028/29)
findings.detail: The full Council report confirms a projected 3-year funding gap of £34.812 Million. The council acknowledges that cash flat revenue funding settlements are forecast for 2027/28 and 2028/29, creating compounding budget pressures beyond this year.
findings.matters: A persistent, multi-year structural deficit signals the council will struggle to fund services without recurring savings; this affects creditworthiness and borrowing risk.
findings.figures: £34.812 Million over three years
findings.quote: the projected 3 year funding gap for the period 2026/27 – 2028/29 is £34.812 Million

findings.matters: Leadership instability during a financial crisis reduces institutional knowledge and execution capability when the Council most needs coherent financial strategy

findings.detail: Health & Social Care Scotland indicates IJBs face an estimated £560m funding gap in 2025/26, described in this report as 'now viewed as likely to be an under-estimate.' COSLA has called on Scottish Government to invest an additional £750m per annum into social care as part of its 2026 Manifesto, framing this as a political choice rather than a settled policy issue.
findings.matters: Signals that Dumfries and Galloway's financial pressures are structural and national, dependent on Scottish Government spending decisions that remain contested and unresolved

findings.matters: Indicates Dumfries and Galloway operates in a sector where most bodies have exhausted their financial buffers, leaving little margin for error or unexpected demand spikes

findings.paper_title: NOM - Health and Social Care Emergency in Dumfries and Galloway Report
findings.headline: Delayed hospital discharges surged 56% in 10 weeks despite the Council continuing to overspend significantly on social care
findings.detail: Between 13 September and 23 November 2025, delayed discharge bed days increased from 3,470 to 5,405 days. The paper explicitly states this deterioration is occurring 'despite the level of spending on health and social care services remaining significantly above the budgeted levels for services delegated by both the NHS and the Council,' and notes current delayed discharges at DGRI alone now equal two of eight wards.
findings.matters: Service performance is deteriorating while the Council spends above budget, indicating systemic inefficiency rather than mere demand growth—a marker of deeper service delivery problems
findings.figures: 5,405 delayed discharge days (23 Nov 2025) vs 3,470 days (13 Sept 2025); increase of 1,935 days (+56%); over 60 delayed discharges at DGRI

The remaining £8.7m relates to Council-delegated services, for which no additional funding has been indicated and which is being addressed only through 'an agreed savings plan being progressed to seek to address this overspend.'
findings.matters: This is a material, direct hit to the Council's own budget with an unresolved spending plan

findings.detail: The council states that delivery of the existing capital programme 'will be extremely challenging within existing available professional and technical resources', particularly given other commitments (Levelling Up, Borderlands Growth Deal). Recruitment of experienced project managers 'has proved very challenging in recent years'. External procurement of skilled staff is also difficult 'particularly in rural areas such as Dumfries and Galloway'.
findings.matters: Understaffed capital programmes deliver late and over budget. This is an execution risk that could translate into further cost escalations and delays, putting additional pressure on an already exhausted capital strategy and worsening the revenue budget position.
