findings.paper_title: Development of Capital Investment Strategy Report FINAL
findings.headline: Capital programme already more than 50% financed by borrowing, with loan charges set to increase further
findings.detail: Over half the current capital investment strategy is funded through borrowing rather than grant or revenue. The paper warns that 'loan charges are already forecast to increase over the upcoming period' and that any additional borrowing compounds this. This high leverage limits capacity to finance further capital projects.
findings.matters: A lender assesses debt profile and capacity. A council already at >50% self-financed capital with rising debt charges has less buffer and less flexibility to handle new requirements or economic stress.
findings.figures: Over 50% of current capital strategy financed by borrowing
findings.quote: over 50% of the current Capital Investment Strategy is already financed through borrowing and the associated loan charges are already forecast to increase over the upcoming period.

findings.paper_title: Development of Capital Investment Strategy Report FINAL
findings.headline: Loan charges already increasing across capital programme, with additional borrowing carrying steep costs
findings.detail: The paper projects that at current interest rates, borrowing costs approximately £70k per annum per £1M over 25 years. It provides an example: £20M additional borrowing spread over 5 years would result in cumulative loan charges rising to £1.4M per annum by year 6 onwards. Loan charges are already forecast to increase 'over the coming period' across the existing programme.
findings.matters: A lender monitors debt service as a proportion of revenue budget. With £36M revenue gap and loan charges already rising, any new borrowing adds material pressure to an already-stressed budget. The council's debt sustainability is the binding constraint.
findings.figures: £70k per annum per £1M borrowed (25-year average); £20M new borrowing = cumulative additional loan charges of £1.4M per annum
findings.quote: Based on current interest rates, the cost of borrowing (written off over an average of 25 years) is around £70k per annum per £1Million

findings.paper_title: Development of Capital Investment Strategy Report FINAL
findings.headline: Council faces a £36 million revenue funding gap over the next three years, severely constraining ability to borrow for capital
findings.detail: With resources forecast to 'continue reducing', the council projects a £36M funding gap over three years. This gap is why the paper emphasises the 'scope for additional borrowing is very limited'. Additional borrowing would require identifying savings beyond already 'very challenging' required levels. This is the structural constraint that makes capital cost escalations unaffordable.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know the council cannot simply borrow its way out of capital problems because its core revenue position is deteriorating. Debt service on new borrowing would worsen an already critical gap.
findings.figures: £36 Million funding gap over the next 3 years
findings.quote: It is important to recognise that the Council's resources are forecast to continue reducing and there is currently a projected Funding gap of £36 Million over the next 3 years.

findings.paper_title: Development of Capital Investment Strategy Report FINAL
findings.headline: Capital investment strategy has exhausted spare capacity with no room to absorb further costs or emergencies
findings.detail: The council explicitly states it has 'very limited flexibility remaining' in its 10-year strategy. The Kirkcudbright Bridge replacement, an unforeseen requirement, is 'currently anticipated will fully utilise the level of flexibility identified', leaving 'very little flexibility for increased spending' within affordability limits. Any new commitments require additional borrowing.
findings.matters: A council with no buffer for new requirements or delivery slippage has higher financial risk. Every emerging need becomes a borrowing decision against an already constrained revenue budget.
findings.figures: £35.2M unallocated over the 10-year period 2026/27–2035/36, but mostly in the latter years
findings.quote: The current Capital Investment Strategy has very limited flexibility remaining, therefore any additional commitments to the programme would result in the need to undertake additional borrowing that would increase the resultant loan charges in the revenue budget.

findings.paper_title: Development of Capital Investment Strategy Report FINAL
findings.headline: Whitesands Flood Protection Scheme costs increase by £8.7M, raising council's share from £5M to £13.7M
findings.detail: The projected scheme cost has escalated to £68.6M. The council's 20% contribution is increasing by £8.7M. The paper states a decision on the progression and funding is required now to comply with Scottish Government funding deadlines. This is a material cost overrun (74% increase in the council's share) on a strategic project.
findings.matters: A major project cost escalation of this magnitude signals either scope creep or initial underestimation, both red flags for a lender reviewing the council's capital planning and delivery capability.
findings.figures: Scheme cost £68.6M; council contribution rising from £5M to £13.7M (£8.7M increase)
findings.quote: the projected Scheme cost has increased to £68.6M and that the progression of the scheme will require an increase in the Council's 20% contribution to the scheme of £8.7M (from £5M to £13.7M)

findings.headline: Care package recycling measures are creating pressures on NHS patient flow and delayed discharges
findings.detail: The IJB's strategy to control costs by recycling (reducing) care packages is having unintended consequences within the wider health and social care system. The report notes that "pressures across the wider care system, including NHS patient flow and delayed discharges, are being adversely affected" and has introduced "additional operational and administrative demands". Collaborative discussions are underway but no resolution is documented.
findings.matters: This creates system risk beyond the IJB's own budget. If the approach is unsustainable with NHS, either the Council and IJB must reverse course (increasing costs) or escalate the conflict, both of which pose governance and financial risk.
findings.figures: 571 hours per week reduction in care-at-home hours since 1 September; 50%–90% recycling rates depending on care group
findings.quote: Pressures across the wider care system, including NHS patient flow and delayed discharges, are being adversely affected by the current care package management process. These challenges have also introduced additional operational and administrative demands.

findings.headline: Savings measures implemented in Q2 are insufficient to bridge the £8.69m gap
findings.detail: The IJB implemented a care-recycling process from 1 September 2025 that projected to deliver £2.174m in savings. However, the report explicitly states these savings, even if the projected full-year run rate (up to £6.5m) is achieved, "would remain above the approved budgetary levels". No further savings measures are detailed that would close the remaining gap.
findings.matters: The council faces a closing window: savings identified will not solve the problem, and no alternative plan is presented. This means either the IJB must achieve unplanned further cuts, or the Council absorbs the overspend.
findings.figures: £2.174m projected savings from recycling; potential £4.4m–£6.5m if trends continue; but £8.69m gap remains
findings.quote: The savings identified to date, including current care reduction and recycling measures are insufficient to balance the budget.

findings.headline: Mental Health service overspend worsened by £386k in Q2 due to expensive residential placements
findings.detail: Mental Health services are forecasting a £2.243m overspend for the year, which has deteriorated by £386k since Q1. The specific driver is additional expensive residential home placements, suggesting either increasing acuity or limited capacity in less expensive service options.
findings.matters: Like Physical Disability, this shows a shift toward more expensive care provision with no indication the trend can be reversed within the current budget envelope.
findings.figures: £2.243m overspend; deteriorated £386k from Q1
findings.quote: Mental Health is currently projected to return an overspend of £2.243million this financial year. This position has deteriorated since Q1 by £386k, which is due to additional expensive residential home placements.

findings.headline: Physical Disability services deteriorated sharply in Q2 due to continued reliance on expensive care agencies
findings.detail: Physical Disability services are forecasting a £2.558m overspend, which has worsened by £565k since Q1. The Council identifies the driver: continued use of expensive care agencies rather than in-house or alternative provision. The service is described as "working hard" to find alternatives, indicating the current position is reactive rather than resolved.
findings.matters: This deterioration suggests the IJB does not have sufficient capacity or workforce to deliver care at budgeted cost, creating an ongoing exposure that may not resolve within this financial year.
findings.figures: £2.558m overspend; deteriorated £565k from Q1
findings.quote: The people with a Physical Disability service are currently projected to return an overspend of £2.558m. This position has deteriorated since Q1 by £565k, which is due to the continued use of expensive care agencies.

findings.headline: Learning Disability services are the largest source of overspend at £5.166m, worsening since Q1
findings.detail: Learning Disability support is forecasting a £5.166m overspend this year. The position has deteriorated by £260k since Q1. The specific driver is that while overall client numbers have declined, the hours of care delivered to remaining clients have increased, suggesting higher-acuity placements or extended support.
findings.matters: This is the largest single service overspend and shows a structural problem (rising hours despite falling client numbers) rather than a temporary pressure, suggesting the underlying cost base is not under control.
findings.figures: £5.166m overspend; deteriorated £260k from Q1
findings.quote: Learning Disability support is currently projected to return an overspend of £5.166 million this financial year. This position has deteriorated since Q1 by £260k. Whilst overall numbers of clients have come down in this area, the number of overall hours of care delivered to clients has increased.

findings.headline: The Council must cover an £8.69m overspend on delegated adult social care services
findings.detail: The Integration Joint Board is forecasting an £8.69m overspend on Council-delegated services for 2025/26 (before applying expected savings; £11.507m before any savings). Under the integration scheme, the IJB must request additional funds from the Council to balance this deficit. This represents a direct and material financial liability to the Council's budget.
findings.matters: A lender or finance director needs to know when a council faces a budget liability it must absorb. This overspend is locked in by the integration scheme and cannot be negotiated away.
findings.figures: £8.69m overspend forecast; £11.507m before savings delivered
findings.quote: the potential significance of Integration Joint Board (IJB) overspending on services delegated by the Council in 2025/26, which is currently forecasting an £8.69m overspend

findings.headline: Children with Disabilities service forecast to overspend by £223k due to complex case requiring extended support into Adult Social Care
findings.detail: An additional overspend of £223k has emerged from a complex case requiring continued support through transition into Adult Social Care. While described as non-recurring, it demonstrates vulnerability of social care budgets to individual case complexity and cost escalation.
findings.matters: Shows that even outside the residential placements pressure area, the service faces unexpected cost drivers from individual cases that breach budget allocations.
findings.quote: The Children with Disabilities service is currently anticipated to return an overspend of £223k this financial year due to additional provision required to support a complex case transition into Adult Social Care.

findings.headline: Risk of further overspend deterioration as residential placement demand is demand-led and new cases may emerge
findings.detail: The council explicitly acknowledges risk that the £477k projected overspend may increase further should demand for children's residential placements continue to increase. The service has limited control over case numbers and costs, and even recent placements ending have been offset by new cases and cost increases.
findings.matters: A lender assesses the predictability of the council's financial position. Demand-led services with acknowledged upside risk create uncertainty about year-end outturn and potential need for emergency funding.
findings.figures: Q2 overspend £477k, subject to increase risk from uncontrolled demand
findings.quote: The risk that this projected overspend may increase further should demand for Children Residential Placements continue to increase and that this position will be subject to increased scrutiny and close budget monitoring to seek to manage this risk and contain spending within the allocated resources

findings.headline: Overall Social Work Services overspend of £477k is masked by inability to fill staffing vacancies due to national social worker shortage
findings.detail: The council's ability to contain the overall Social Work Services overspend to £477k depends on £651k underspending on staff costs caused by unfilled positions in a national shortage of qualified social workers. This means the underlying demand-driven overspend is much larger and is being offset by vacancy rather than genuine savings. The mitigation is fragile and dependent on continued recruitment challenges.
findings.matters: Lenders need to understand whether financial improvements are structural or cyclical. Mitigation through vacancies is temporary and cannot be relied upon, suggesting underlying structural pressure that will emerge when positions are filled.
findings.figures: £477k overall overspend, £651k staffing underspend, implying underlying £1.128 million pressure
findings.quote: it is expected that other variances across the wider Social Work Services budget, including projected underspending on staff costs, will offset the overall overspend on residential placements by the end of the financial year. There continues to be a national shortage of qualified social workers, making recruitment to skilled vacant posts challenging.

findings.headline: Children's residential placements forecast to overspend by £1.196 million despite £3 million additional budget, representing 58% expenditure increase from prior year
findings.detail: The council allocated £3 million in additional budget pressure funding for residential placements in 2025/26. Despite this, the service is forecast to overspend by £1.196 million on this area alone. The overspend forecast has increased by a further £222k since Q1. As of 31 October 2025, there were 35 children in residential placements against a budgeted target of 28. The 58% increase in expenditure compared to 2023/24 indicates structural demand growth.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand whether the council can manage its spending commitments. This shows demand-led costs that are outpacing budget allocations and mitigation efforts, potentially requiring drawdown of reserves or further borrowing.
findings.figures: £1.196 million overspend, 58% increase from 2023/24, £222k increase from Q1, 35 children in placements vs 28 target, £3 million additional budget allocated
findings.quote: it is currently forecast that Children Residential Placements will return an overspend of £1.196 Million representing a 58% increase in expenditure from 2023/24. This forecast overspend has risen by a further £222k from quarter 1

findings.committee: South West of Scotland Transport Partnership (SWestrans)
findings.headline: Unplanned interim costs of £18k for school transport following implementation issues
findings.detail: Interim amendments were needed on the 246 route to support school transport after the new bus arrangements began on 7 August 2025. These temporary measures are still under review and are expected to cost approximately £18k until Christmas, indicating that the initial service design did not meet actual demand.
findings.matters: Service implementation has revealed unexpected costs and operational shortfalls, suggesting the actual cost of bus provision may exceed initial assumptions.
findings.figures: Approximately £18k additional costs until Christmas break
findings.quote: This has included the implementation of interim amendments to the 246 route at school times to support non-entitled pupils travelling to Wallace Hall Academy, running Monday to Friday, while alternative long-term solutions are reviewed and discussed with colleagues in the Council and the commercial operator. While these interim arrangements are subject to ongoing review, it is currently assumed that additional costs of approximately £18k will be incurred up until the Christmas break.

findings.committee: South West of Scotland Transport Partnership (SWestrans)
findings.headline: Dumfries and Galloway Council now operating bus routes as 'operator of last resort' with unresolved costs
findings.detail: Following a tender process, DGC has taken on bus routes where commercial operators did not bid. The document explicitly states that the cost of these services is 'still subject to ongoing review and may change as assumptions and estimates are refined', and this refinement 'may result in a change to the funding levels and associated requisition requirements'. This means the cost to D&G of meeting its bus service obligations is currently uncertain.
findings.matters: D&G is directly exposed to bus operation costs and risks; if SWestrans cannot cover DGC costs from current resources, the council will face an increased requisition demand.
findings.figures: Total resources available to SWestrans: £4,838,786 in 2025/26
findings.quote: The cost of the provision of DGC buses provided by Dumfries and Galloway Council is still subject to ongoing review and may change as assumptions and estimates are refined. This refinement may result in a change to the funding levels and associated requisition requirements reflected within the Appendix.

findings.headline: Ambitious capital programme including a new secondary school commits the council to sustained high borrowing over at least two years
findings.detail: The 2025/26 Treasury Strategy identified a £23.5m borrowing requirement for that year with 'further borrowing being required in 2026/27'. The capital projects driving this include a new Dumfries High School, Dumfries Academy Refurbishment and Loreburn Primary relocation, Roads Investment, and a Dumfries Zero Waste Park.
findings.matters: Large capital commitments lock in substantial borrowing and interest costs for multiple years ahead, reducing the council's financial flexibility and increasing debt service burden.
findings.figures: £23.5m borrowing requirement 2025/26; further borrowing required 2026/27 (quantum not specified)
findings.quote: the borrowing requirement for 2025/26 would increase by around £23.5M, with further borrowing being required in 2026/27. This additional borrowing is to fund the ambitious Capital Investment Strategy which includes the new Dumfries High School, Dumfries Academy Refurbishment/Loreburn Primary relocation, Roads Investment and the Dumfries Zero Waste Park.

findings.headline: Council has borrowed short-term (1-5 years) betting on interest rate falls; if rates stay elevated, refinancing costs will spike
findings.detail: All external loans taken in 2024/25 were for 1 to 5 year duration because longer-term rates were elevated. The strategy assumes rates will 'fall back over the immediate term' to allow cheaper refinancing when this debt matures. Average borrowing cost is 4.6% and net interest paid totalled £10.517m.
findings.matters: If interest rates remain elevated or rise further, the council faces significantly higher refinancing costs when £6.3m of temporary debt and short-term loans mature, worsening the budget position.
findings.figures: Temporary debt £6.338m at 4.070%; net interest paid £10.517m in 2024/25; average interest rate 4.6%
findings.quote: All external loans were taken for a 1 to 5 year duration, as longer term interest rates remained elevated. Forecasts suggest that longer term rates will continue to fall back over the immediate term, therefore, it is anticipated that we will be able to replace this borrowing at the end of the loan term with lower rate borrowing

findings.headline: Investment income has fallen 45% year-on-year as cash reserves continue to deplete
findings.detail: Investment income fell from £2.474m in 2023/24 to £1.351m in 2024/25. The council attributes this to 'reducing cash balances and falling interest rates.' The report references falling reserve levels as previously reported to the committee in June as part of the 2024/25 outturn.
findings.matters: Declining reserves reduce the council's financial flexibility to absorb shocks or manage unplanned spending, increasing reliance on borrowing at potentially higher rates.
findings.figures: Investment income £1.351m (2024/25) vs £2.474m (2023/24); 45% decrease
findings.quote: This is lower than the £2.474Million received in 2023/24 due to reducing cash balances and falling interest rates.

findings.headline: Net external debt rose by £56.6m in one year and the council has reversed five years of debt reduction with further rises planned
findings.detail: Actual Net External Debt increased from £147.823m to £204.390m in 2024/25. The council states this 'is reversing the significant reductions in borrowing the Council has seen over the past 5 years' and notes that 'borrowing will continue to increase over the immediate term', with a further £23.5m borrowing requirement planned for 2025/26.
findings.matters: A fundamental shift from deleveraging to re-leveraging changes the council's debt trajectory and exposes it to sustained high interest costs and refinancing risk.
findings.figures: Net external debt £147.823m (2023/24) to £204.390m (2024/25); planned £23.5m additional borrowing 2025/26
findings.quote: This increase in borrowing is reversing the significant reductions in borrowing the Council has seen over the past 5 years and it is anticipated that borrowing will continue to increase over the immediate term.

findings.paper_title: Social Work Services Q4 Revenue Budget Monitoring 202425 Report
findings.headline: Foster carer recruitment continues to fail due to national shortage; external placements growing, costs rising
findings.detail: Fostering allowances overspent by £204k due to increased external placements, directly linked to failure to recruit and retain local foster carers. The service is continuing recruitment campaigns but acknowledges this is "extremely challenging" and notes it is "following the national trend." External placements cost more than internal ones.
findings.matters: A key mitigation strategy—recruiting more local foster carers to reduce external placement costs—is not working, meaning costs will continue to rise and this pressure will persist.
findings.figures: £204k overspend in fostering allowances
findings.quote: fostering allowances returned an overspend of £204k due to the increased number of external placements that have been required, related to the ongoing challenges to recruit and retain foster carers. The service is continuing with the recruitment campaign for local foster carers, however, following the national trend this is proving to be extremely challenging.

findings.paper_title: Social Work Services Q4 Revenue Budget Monitoring 202425 Report
findings.headline: Council abandoned planned reductions in residential placements and allocated additional £3 Million for 2025/26, bringing total residential budget to £8.520 Million
findings.detail: The paper explicitly states that "the previously planned reductions in the number of Children's Residential Placements will no longer be achievable." Rather than address demand management, the council applied an additional £3 million to the 2025/26 budget beyond any investment measures, targeting 28 children in residential placements. Even this increased allocation is described as requiring "close monitoring and review" due to ongoing pressures.
findings.matters: The council is capitulating to uncontrolled demand and scaling budgets to match it rather than constraining costs or changing the service model. The need for continued close monitoring implies uncertainty about even this higher allocation being sufficient.
findings.figures: £3 Million additional allocation for 2025/26; £8.520 Million total residential placement budget; target of 28 children
findings.quote: the previously planned reductions in the number of Children's Residential Placements will no longer be achievable. In recognition of the previously agreed reductions not being achievable, updated projections were agreed by the Enabling and Customer Services committee... additional resources of £3 Million, beyond the additional investment measures reflected in the budget from 2024/25, have been applied to the Social Work Services budget for 2025/26. This increases the total 2025/26 budget allocated for Children's Residential Placements to £8.520 million.

findings.paper_title: Social Work Services Q4 Revenue Budget Monitoring 202425 Report
findings.headline: £691k of the £1.112 Million planned investment measures did not materialise, leaving no delivery buffer for residential placement pressures
findings.detail: The council had agreed £1.112 million of investment measures to mitigate placement pressures, including £413k for Intensive Foster Carers (£0 spent) and £394k for an Outreach Support Team (£154k spent). Only £421k was actually spent against the plan. The underspend was then used to partially offset the overspends rather than delivering the intended mitigation.
findings.matters: Failed implementation of agreed savings and mitigation strategies means the council cannot execute its own budget plans, suggesting either planning failure or capacity constraints in delivery.
findings.figures: £1.112 Million planned; £421k actual spend; £691k underspend; Intensive Foster Carers £413k planned, £0 spent
findings.quote: there were some delays/challenges associated with the implementation of the agreed measures, resulting in expenditure of £421k being incurred against the agreed £1.112 Million

findings.paper_title: Social Work Services Q4 Revenue Budget Monitoring 202425 Report
findings.headline: Children's residential placements exceeded target by 11 young people, driving £2.287 Million overspend
findings.detail: The service had 32 young people in residential placements against a target of 21—a 52% overrun. This overspend was driven by both increased numbers and higher average cost per placement due to case complexity. The paper notes this was "slightly higher than previously estimated due to increases in the cost of individual placement packages during the last quarter."
findings.matters: Continued and accelerating demand for high-cost placements signals the council cannot manage this pressure within its budgeted baseline, and planned reductions are now deemed unachievable.
findings.figures: 32 actual vs 21 target; £2,287k overspend; increased cost per placement due to complexity
findings.quote: Residential Placements overspent by £2,287k against the agreed allocated resources due to an increase in the number of children requiring a residential placement and an increase in the average cost of individual placements (due to the complexity of cases being presented). There were 32 young people in Residential Placements at the end of the financial year, which was 11 above the agreed target (21)

findings.paper_title: Social Work Services Q4 Revenue Budget Monitoring 202425 Report
findings.headline: £1.913 Million drawn from Social Work Budget Pressures reserve to achieve balanced budget
findings.detail: The council applied nearly £2 million from its reserves to balance Social Work Services' budget for 2024/25. This was part of a planned £3.276 million non-recurring allocation expected to cover pressures over 2023/24 to 2025/26. The reliance on reserves rather than permanent budget solutions indicates the overspends are structural.
findings.matters: Using reserves to plug recurring budget gaps is not sustainable and reduces financial flexibility for future years and unforeseen pressures.
findings.figures: £1.913 Million applied from reserves; £3.276 Million total allocation across three years
findings.quote: resources of £1.913 Million have been applied to Social Work Services from the agreed Council's 'Social Work Budget Pressures funding' within reserves
